title: Why do we laugh
paragraphs: What makes you laugh the most?
While rib-tickling jokes and hilarious videos certainly do make us giggle, most of the time we laugh because of something much simpler: being with other people.

So much so that we are 30 times more likely to laugh when we're with others, according to a study by neuroscientist Robert Provine from the University of Maryland. "When you're alone, laughter basically disappears," he told Smithsonian Magazine.
So, what is it about other people that makes us split our sides? The answer lies deep within our brains, and in how we form communities.

Laughter is a social emotion that we use to "make and maintain social bonds," says Professor Sophie Smith from University College London in an article for the BBC. It reassures people that situations are non-threatening. Those who laugh frequently are also often more popular. Even in a normal conversation we laugh seven times every 10 minutes, she says.

Professor Smith also explains that laughter is very different to speech. It is non-verbal: the wheezing and snorting sounds are produced by air being pushed out quickly at high pressure, without involving the teeth or lips. These sounds are the kind we make when in a state of heightened emotion.

In this respect, laughter sounds more like an animal call than human language. This theory is backed up by tests which show the part of the brain responsible for laughter is not the neocortex used in language, but an 'older' area we share with mammals.

Indeed, chimpanzees, gorillas and even rats all enjoy a good chortle, especially when being tickled. Just be careful when you tickle a gorilla, or you might end up laughing on the other side of your face... (Did you laugh at that gag? Or did it just make you groan?)

vocabulary.entry: rib-tickling [adj.] /ˈrɪb tɪklɪŋ/ 非常有趣的；令人捧腹大笑的 (口语)
vocabulary.example: He told a rib-tickling story about his trip.
vocabulary.translation: 他讲了一个关于他旅行的非常有趣的故事。

vocabulary.entry: hilarious [adj.] /hɪˈleəriəs/ 极其滑稽的；非常有趣的
vocabulary.translation: 这场喜剧表演非常滑稽。

vocabulary.example: The children giggled at the funny cartoon.
vocabulary.translation: 孩子们看着有趣的卡通片咯咯地笑。

vocabulary.entry: split our sides [phr.] /splɪt ˈaʊə saɪdz/ 捧腹大笑 (口语；固定搭配)
vocabulary.example: The joke made us split our sides.
vocabulary.translation: 这个笑话让我们捧腹大笑。

vocabulary.entry: make and maintain social bonds [phr.] /meɪk ənd meɪnˈteɪn ˈsəʊʃəl bɒndz/ 建立和维护社会联系 (固定搭配)
vocabulary.example: Team activities help make and maintain social bonds.
vocabulary.translation: 团队活动有助于建立和维护社会联系。

vocabulary.example: Body language is a form of non-verbal communication.
vocabulary.translation: 肢体语言是一种非语言交流形式。

vocabulary.example: The old man's wheezing could be heard across the room.
vocabulary.translation: 整个房间都能听到老人的喘息声。

vocabulary.example: The horse's snorting scared the children.
vocabulary.translation: 马的喷鼻声吓坏了孩子们。

vocabulary.entry: heightened emotion [n.] /ˈhaɪtənd ɪˈməʊʃən/ 情绪高涨 (固定搭配)
vocabulary.example: In a state of heightened emotion, he said things he regretted.
vocabulary.translation: 在情绪高涨的状态下，他说了些后悔的话。

vocabulary.entry: back up [phr.] /bæk ʌp/ 支持；证实 (固定搭配)
vocabulary.example: The evidence backs up his claim.

vocabulary.entry: neocortex [n.] /ˌniːəʊˈkɔːteks/ 新皮质 (神经科学词汇)
vocabulary.example: The neocortex is involved in higher-order thinking.

vocabulary.term: laugh on the other side of your face [phr.]
vocabulary.entry: laugh on the other side of your face [phr.] /lɑːf ɒn ði ˈʌðə saɪd əv jɔː feɪs/ 转喜为忧 (口语；固定搭配)
vocabulary.example: He thought he had won, but he was laughing on the other side of his face when the results came out.
vocabulary.translation: 他以为自己赢了，但结果出来后他就转喜为忧了。

vocabulary.entry: gag [n.] /ɡæɡ/ 玩笑；插科打诨 (口语)
vocabulary.example: His gag made the audience laugh.
The bad joke made everyone groan.
vocabulary.translation: 这个糟糕的笑话让每个人都叹息。
